lessons.title: Causes of Segregation in Blends
lessons.body: Segregation happens when particles in a blended fertilizer separate by size, shape, or density. In Africa, many blenders use simple drum mixers or shovel mixing, which can cause segregation if not controlled. The main causes are: differences in particle size, differences in density, and handling methods like pouring or dropping from height. For example, if you blend urea (prills, 2-4 mm) with rock phosphate (powder, <1 mm), the fine powder sifts through the gaps between prills, sinking to the bottom. This is called sifting segregation. Another cause is fluidization: when you pour a blend from a height, air resistance affects light particles more, blowing them away from heavy ones. In a typical African warehouse, a blend of 50 kg urea, 50 kg DAP, and 50 kg MOP dropped from a 2-meter height can segregate by up to 20% in nutrient content from top to bottom of the pile. Vibration during transport on rough roads also causes smaller particles to move downward. Moisture makes it worse: damp urea sticks together while dry MOP stays separate. To avoid segregation, you must match particle sizes (within 1 mm difference) and avoid free-fall drops. Always test your blend by sampling from top, middle, and bottom of a bag or pile to see if segregation is happening.

lessons.title: Particle Size Distribution and Its Impact
lessons.body: Particle size distribution (PSD) is the range of sizes of particles in your fertilizer materials. If all particles are the same size, they mix evenly and stay mixed. But in reality, each fertilizer has a different PSD. For example, urea prills are typically 2-4 mm, DAP granules are 2-4 mm, but MOP (muriate of potash) can be 1-3 mm, and some local rock phosphates are powder (<0.5 mm). The wider the PSD, the more segregation you get. A good rule: the largest particle should not be more than 1.5 times the smallest. So if your smallest is 1 mm, largest should be 1.5 mm. To measure PSD, use a set of sieves (e.g., 1 mm, 2 mm, 3 mm, 4 mm) and shake a 500 g sample for 5 minutes. Weigh what stays on each sieve. In Africa, many blenders skip this test. But a simple sieve set costs about $50 and saves money. If your PSD is too wide, you can screen out fines or crush oversize particles. You can also buy fertilizers with similar PSD. For example, blend urea (2-4 mm) with DAP (2-4 mm) and MOP (2-4 mm) â all from the same supplier. Avoid blending powder with prills unless you first granulate the powder. Remember: uniform size means uniform blend.

lessons.title: Preventing Segregation During Handling
lessons.body: Even a perfect blend will segregate if you handle it badly. In Africa, common handling mistakes include pouring from height, using augers, and dropping bags. Here is how to prevent segregation: First, never drop blend from more than 1 meter. Use a chute or lower the bag slowly. Second, avoid conveyor belts that cause vibration â instead use bucket elevators or gentle screw conveyors with full flights. Third, when loading into a truck, pour the blend in one spot and let it form a pile, then level it â do not pour from the side. Fourth, minimize transfers: each transfer increases segregation. If you must transfer, use a closed system. Fifth, keep moisture low â if blend is damp, particles stick and segregate less, but too damp causes caking. Aim for 1-2% moisture. Sixth, use a ribbon blender or paddle mixer instead of a drum mixer â they cause less segregation. Seventh, after blending, bag immediately and store bags flat, not stacked too high (max 8 bags high). Eighth, when applying in the field, do not broadcast by hand from a height â use a cyclone spreader or drop spreader at low height. Finally, train workers: a simple rule like 'no pouring from shoulder height' can reduce segregation by 30%. Test your handling by sampling from different parts of a truckload after transport.

lessons.title: Evaluating Blend Quality by Segregation Tests
lessons.body: To know if your blend is uniform, you must test it. The simplest test is the 'bag sampling test'. Take 10 bags from a production run. From each bag, take three samples: top, middle, and bottom (using a scoop or thief sampler). Mix each sample separately, then send to a lab for nutrient analysis (N, P, K). If the nutrient content varies by more than 10% between top and bottom of the same bag, you have segregation. A cheaper field test: use a 'segregation column'. Fill a 1-meter tall pipe (10 cm diameter) with blend, then vibrate it for 5 minutes on a vibrating table or by tapping. Then carefully remove the blend in 10 cm layers and weigh each layer. If the ratio of fine to coarse particles changes by more than 15% from top to bottom, segregation is high. Another test: the 'sieve test' â take a 1 kg sample, sieve it into size fractions, and check if the proportion of each fertilizer matches the original recipe. For example, if your recipe is 50% urea, 30% DAP, 20% MOP, then each sieve fraction should have similar ratios. In Africa, you can do a simple 'salt test': mix 1 kg blend with 1 liter of water, stir, and let settle. The fertilizer that dissolves first (urea) will be in the top water layer, while sand-like particles (MOP) sink. This gives a rough idea. Record all results and adjust your blending if variation is above 10%.

lessons.title: Strategies for Improving Blend Homogeneity
lessons.body: To get a homogeneous blend, you need the right recipe, right equipment, and right method. First, match particle sizes: buy fertilizers with similar PSD. If not possible, screen out fines below 1 mm and oversize above 4 mm. Second, use a proper mixer: a horizontal ribbon blender or a paddle mixer runs at 20-30 rpm for 3-5 minutes. Do not overmix â that causes segregation. Third, add liquids (like water or oil) at 1-2% to reduce dust and stick particles together. Fourth, use a 'master batch' approach: pre-blend small amounts of minor nutrients with a carrier (like sand) before adding to the main mix. Fifth, load the mixer correctly: add the largest particles first, then medium, then fine. Sixth, control moisture: keep blend at 1-2% moisture by storing in dry conditions. Seventh, use anti-segregation additives like clay or starch at 0.5-1% â they coat particles and reduce separation. Eighth, after mixing, test uniformity by sampling from 5 points in the mixer. Ninth, bag immediately and avoid drops. Tenth, train workers on gentle handling. In Africa, a simple improvement is to use a cement mixer (rented for $20/day) instead of shovel mixing â it gives 40% better uniformity. Another low-cost method: mix on a clean concrete floor by rolling a drum back and forth for 10 minutes. Always aim for a coefficient of variation (CV) below 10% for N, P, and K.

lessons.title: Case Studies of Segregation Issues
lessons.body: Case 1: In Kenya, a blender mixed 100 kg urea (2-4 mm) with 50 kg rock phosphate powder (<0.5 mm) in a drum mixer. After 5 minutes, they bagged and sold to farmers. Farmers reported yellow patches (urea) and white patches (rock phosphate) in the field. Sampling showed nitrogen varied from 18% to 32% between bags. Solution: they switched to granulated rock phosphate (2-4 mm) and used a ribbon blender. Variation dropped to 5%. Case 2: In Nigeria, a cooperative blended 200 kg NPK 20-10-10 using shovel mixing on a concrete floor. They poured from a height of 2 meters into bags. After transport on rough roads, the bottom of each bag had 30% more MOP (heavy) and the top had more urea (light). Farmers complained of poor growth. Solution: they built a simple chute to lower bags and used a cement mixer. Segregation reduced by 60%. Case 3: In South Africa, a large blender used a conveyor belt to move blend to a bagging hopper. Vibration caused fines to settle, so the first 10 bags had 25% more fines than the last 10. Solution: they replaced the belt with a bucket elevator and added a re-mixer before bagging. Uniformity improved to CV 8%. Case 4: In Tanzania, a farmer mixed DAP and urea by hand in a bucket and applied by broadcasting. He saw uneven crop growth. Solution: he now mixes in a closed drum for 5 minutes and applies with a drop spreader. Yield increased by 20%. These cases show that simple, low-cost changes â matching particle sizes, gentle handling, and proper mixing â solve most segregation problems.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of sifting segregation in fertilizer blends?
quiz.explanation: Smaller particles sift through gaps between larger particles, causing separation.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer material is most likely to cause segregation when blended with urea prills?
quiz.explanation: Powder is much smaller than prills and will sift through, causing severe segregation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum height for dropping a fertilizer blend to prevent segregation?
quiz.explanation: Dropping from more than 1 meter causes air resistance to separate light and heavy particles.

quiz.q: Which handling method is most likely to cause segregation?
options: B) Using a conveyor belt with vibration
quiz.explanation: Vibration on conveyor belts causes smaller particles to move downward, increasing segregation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for a fertilizer blend to reduce segregation?
quiz.explanation: 1-2% moisture reduces dust and sticks particles slightly, minimizing segregation without causing caking.

quiz.q: Which test can be used to evaluate blend uniformity in the field?
quiz.explanation: Both sieve and salt tests are simple field methods to check segregation.

quiz.q: What does a coefficient of variation (CV) below 10% indicate for a fertilizer blend?
quiz.explanation: CV below 10% means nutrient content is consistent across samples, indicating good uniformity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum difference in particle size between fertilizers in a blend?
quiz.explanation: Particle sizes should not differ by more than 1 mm to prevent segregation.

quiz.q: Which mixer type is recommended to reduce segregation?
quiz.explanation: Ribbon blenders provide gentle, thorough mixing with less segregation than drum mixers.

quiz.q: What is a 'master batch' in fertilizer blending?
options: B) Pre-blending minor nutrients with a carrier
quiz.explanation: A master batch ensures even distribution of small quantities of nutrients before adding to the main mix.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a strategy to improve blend homogeneity?
quiz.explanation: Pouring from height increases segregation, so it is not a strategy to improve homogeneity.

quiz.q: In the Kenyan case study, what was the main cause of segregation?
options: A) Mixing urea prills with rock phosphate powder
quiz.explanation: The large difference in particle size between urea prills and rock phosphate powder caused sifting segregation.

quiz.q: What simple change reduced segregation in the Nigerian case study?
options: A) Using a chute to lower bags
quiz.explanation: Lowering bags with a chute reduced free-fall and thus segregation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sieving time for particle size distribution analysis?
quiz.explanation: Shaking sieves for 5 minutes ensures proper separation of particle sizes.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT affect segregation?
quiz.explanation: Color does not affect physical segregation; size, shape, and density do.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding 0.5-1% clay or starch to a blend?
quiz.explanation: Clay or starch coats particles and reduces their tendency to separate.

quiz.q: How many bags high should fertilizer bags be stacked to minimize segregation?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 8 bags high can cause pressure and vibration that lead to segregation.

quiz.q: In the South African case study, what caused fines to settle in the first bags?
quiz.explanation: Vibration from the conveyor belt caused smaller particles to settle, affecting the first bags.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a low-cost method to improve mixing in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A rented cement mixer provides better mixing than manual methods at low cost.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sampling method to check for segregation in a bag?
options: A) Take one sample from the top
B) Take samples from top, middle, and bottom
C) Take a sample from the middle only
D) Take a sample from the bottom only
quiz.explanation: Sampling from different depths reveals if segregation has occurred within the bag.

quiz.q: What does a high coefficient of variation (CV) indicate?
quiz.explanation: High CV means nutrient content varies widely, indicating poor blend uniformity.

quiz.q: Which fertilizer is most likely to be the fine fraction in a blend?
quiz.explanation: Rock phosphate is often available as a fine powder, much smaller than prills or granules.

quiz.q: What is the recommended mixing time for a ribbon blender?
quiz.explanation: 3-5 minutes is sufficient for uniform mixing without causing segregation from overmixing.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of segregation in a fertilizer blend?
quiz.explanation: Patches of different colors indicate that particles have separated.

quiz.q: What is the first step in preventing segregation during handling?
quiz.explanation: Reducing drop height minimizes free-fall segregation.

quiz.q: In the Tanzanian case study, what improved yield by 20%?
options: A) Mixing in a closed drum and using a drop spreader
quiz.explanation: Proper mixing and application reduced segregation and improved crop yield.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a segregation column test?
options: C) To evaluate segregation by vibration
quiz.explanation: The column test simulates vibration during transport to assess segregation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of segregation?
quiz.explanation: Color does not affect physical segregation.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum variation in nutrient content between top and bottom of a bag?
quiz.explanation: Variation above 10% indicates significant segregation and poor blend quality.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to take samples from different depths in a bag?
quiz.explanation: A thief sampler (or probe) is designed to extract samples from various depths.
